newsitem.title: USA: Fed's new model called blend of art and science.
newsitem.headline: Fed's new model called blend of art and science.

text.p: The Federal Reserve on Friday unveiled a new computer forecasting model that elevates the role that the expectations of consumers, businesses and investors play in the economy.

The new tool for analysing the nation's economy will be used by economists at the central bank to forecast trends in the economy. The Fed will also use it to evaluate the impact of potential changes in interest rates.

Called the "FRB/US," the updated model replaces an old version the Fed had been using since the 1960s and is the culmination of several years of research. The Fed also has a world economic model looking at the domestic economy in relation to developments in foreign countries.
In addition to discussing the various uses for the models, Fed economists also emphasised such high-tech methods are far from the only tool used in analysing the economy.

In a paper presented at a monetary policy conference, economists David Reifschneider, David Stockton and David Wilcox, said human judgment also plays an important role, making policy-making a blend of art and science.
"Science enters through the use of sophisticated econometrics, rigorous theory and high-speed computers," they said. "Art enters in order to deal with all the short-comings of science."

At the conference, economists praised the new model's focus on how perceptions about growth and inflation can affect the course of the economy, an area of research that has gained a great deal of prominence in the economics profession.
"Economic research of the past few decades has really emphasised the role of expectations," said Allan Meltzer, professor of economics at Carnegie Mellon University.
"It's good to see that the Fed staff is incorporating this into what they're doing," he said.
The concept stems from research by Nobel laureate Robert Lucas on the role of "rational expectations."

Such research pointed to a link between the expectations of financial market players, consumers and companies about high inflation during the 1970s and early 1980s and the difficulty that the Fed had in containing it.

In addition to perceptions about inflation, expectations about government spending and taxes and the overall health of the economy can also affect people's behaviour in ways that affect economic trends.
"Incorporating expectations was a fundamental need for doing the type of analysis that we need to do," said Fed economist John Williams in discussing the computer model.
Williams and his colleagues presented a number of ways the tool would be used.
In one example, the domestic economic model was used to look at whether confidence in a central bank's inflation-fighting resolve made it easier to rein in prices.
The finding was that a high degree of confidence in policy-makers allowed them to drive inflation lower with less of a cost to economic growth.

Such a situation arises when bond markets become accustomed to "anticipating" potential credit tightenings by the central bank. That expectation causes market interest rates to rise, meaning the Fed may not have to clamp down as forcefully on credit.
